title: Missing Number
description: Brute force to optimized: linear search per candidate versus a hash set versus a sum formula versus XOR.

blocks.text: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers taken from the range 0 to n (inclusive), exactly one number in that range is missing from the array. Return that missing number.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Roll Call With One Absent Number
blocks.text: Picture a roll call where every number from 0 to n should answer, but one number never gets called out. Comparing who actually answered against who should have answered reveals exactly which number is missing.

blocks.caption: One number from the range 0 to n never appears in the array

blocks.text: With a single element array, n equals 1, so the range to check is 0 to 1. Since only 0 is present, the missing number is 1.

This looks like another "have I seen this before" problem, but it is worth noticing one thing that makes it different from Contains Duplicate: the complete set of values that should be present is fully known in advance.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Unlike Contains Duplicate, which only needed to detect a repeat, this problem is looking for an absence, one specific value from an entirely known range, 0 to n, that never shows up.

Observation 2: A hash set can track exactly which values are present, the same technique already used for Contains Duplicate, and then checking the full range against it finds the gap directly.

Observation 3: Since the full expected range and its total are both known ahead of time, individual values do not actually need to be tracked at all, only two running numbers, the expected sum and the actual sum, and their difference reveals the missing value directly.

Observation 4: The sum trick can silently overflow for large inputs, but XOR provides the exact same cancellation idea, every present value cancels with its matching index, without ever being able to produce a value larger than the inputs involved.
Recognizing that the full expected range is known in advance is what unlocks two genuinely different constant-space tricks beyond the hash set that Contains Duplicate already established.
For every candidate number from 0 to n, scan the entire array checking whether that candidate is present. The first candidate not found is the missing number.

items: For every candidate from 0 to n, search the whole array for it.
If a candidate is never found, it is the missing number.

codes.python:
def missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    for candidate in range(n + 1):                          # try every number in the expected range
        if candidate not in nums:                             # linear search through the whole array
            return candidate
    return -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [3, 0, 1]
    print(missing_number(nums))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The outer loop covers every candidate in the full expected range, 0 through n inclusive, exactly n plus 1 values.
Each candidate triggers a fresh linear scan through the entire array, with no memory carried over from checking the previous candidate.
The function returns the instant a candidate is not found, since the problem guarantees exactly one such value exists.

blocks.text: Every candidate is checked against the full array, so the one candidate that never appears is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), a full linear search for each of the n plus 1 candidates.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.
Limitation: the array is rescanned from scratch for every single candidate, when a single pass could record everything that is actually present.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the repeated scan works but is wasteful: every one of the n plus 1 candidates re-scans the entire array from scratch, even though the array never changes between checks.

What stays the same as Contains Duplicate: recording every present value once, in a hash set, then checking membership in constant time instead of rescanning.

What is different here: instead of looking for a repeat, the goal is to find the one value from a fully known range that is absent, which the same hash set answers just as directly.

Can this be checked in one pass over the array plus one pass over the range: yes, first record every present value, then walk the full expected range once, checking each candidate against the set.

The core idea: build a hash set of every present value in one pass, then walk the expected range 0 to n and return the first candidate missing from the set.

Record every value that is actually present in a hash set with one pass over the array. Then walk through the expected range 0 to n and return the first value not found in the set. Constant time average set lookups replace the repeated linear scans.
Build a set of every present value, then check the full expected range against it.

blocks.caption: Optimized: record every present value, then find the one missing from the full range

blocks.text: This works because the hash set exactly captures which values from the range are present after a single pass over nums, and since the problem guarantees exactly one value from 0 to n is absent, walking that range once and checking the set is guaranteed to find it, with each check running in constant time on average.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to build the set and one pass to check the range.
Space: O(n), for the set holding every present value.

The sum of every number from 0 to n has a closed form, n times (n plus 1), divided by 2. Subtracting the actual sum of the array from this expected sum leaves exactly the one number that never got added in, with no extra data structure at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["n equals 3, expected sum of 0 to 3","0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6"],["Actual sum of nums","3 + 0 + 1 = 4"],["Missing number","6 minus 4 equals 2"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: subtract the actual sum from the expected sum of the full range

codes.python:
def missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    expected_sum = n * (n + 1) // 2                          # sum of every number from 0 to n
    actual_sum = sum(nums)
    return expected_sum - actual_sum                           # whatever is left over is the missing number


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [3, 0, 1]
    print(missing_number(nums))

items: The expected sum is computed directly from the closed form formula, with no loop needed to add up the range 0 to n.
The actual sum is computed with a single pass over nums, adding up exactly the values that are genuinely present.
Subtracting the actual sum from the expected sum leaves precisely the one value that never contributed to the actual total, the missing number.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass to compute the actual sum.
Space: O(1), only the two running sums are kept, no set needed.
11. Further Optimization: XOR Instead of Sum

The sum formula works, but adding up n numbers can overflow a fixed size integer type when n is very large. XOR sidesteps that entirely: XOR every index from 0 to n minus 1 together with every value in the array, plus n itself. Every present value cancels out with its matching index (since a value XORed with itself is 0), leaving only the missing number, with no risk of overflow since XOR never produces a value larger than the inputs.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: XOR every index and value together, matching pairs cancel out

items: The running result starts at n itself, the one value in the full range 0 to n that has no matching array index to pair with.
Each iteration XORs in both the current index and the current value, so every genuinely present value ends up paired with, and cancelled by, its own index somewhere across the whole pass.
Since XOR is its own inverse, every value that is truly present cancels away completely, leaving only the missing number's contribution behind in the final result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the same single pass.
Space: O(1), and unlike the sum formula, immune to integer overflow regardless of how large n gets.

blocks.text: This problem is a good showcase of three genuinely different constant or linear space tricks for the same result: hashing for clarity, a sum formula for simplicity, and XOR for robustness against overflow.

items: Forgetting that the range to check is 0 to n inclusive, not 0 to n minus 1.
Using the sum formula with a data type too small to hold the sum for large inputs, reintroducing the overflow risk the XOR trick was meant to avoid.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single element array","The missing number is either 0 or 1."],["The missing number being 0 itself, or being n itself","Both are handled by the sum and XOR approaches without special casing."]]}

blocks.text: Lead with the sum formula since it is the most intuitive O(1) space approach, then mention XOR as a follow up when asked about overflow safety for very large inputs.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid extra space", think: the sum formula needs only two running totals, no hash set.
If the interviewer says "what about integer overflow", think: XOR achieves the same cancellation as the sum formula without ever risking overflow.
If the interviewer says "why does XOR work here", think: every present value pairs with and cancels its own index, leaving only the unmatched missing number behind.

Single Number, which reuses this exact XOR cancellation idea in its purest form, every value that appears twice cancels out, leaving only the one that appears once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (sum): O(n) time, O(1) space. Further optimized (XOR): O(n) time, O(1) space, immune to overflow.

items: Pattern: comparing an array against a fully known expected set, using hashing, a closed form sum, or bitwise XOR to find the single value that never showed up.

Core Idea: since the full expected range 0 to n is known in advance, the missing value can be found by hashing every present value, by subtracting the actual sum from the closed form expected sum, or by XORing every index and value together so present values cancel out.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for every optimized version.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the hash set version, O(1) for both the sum and XOR versions.
Most Important Observation: when the full expected set is known in advance, two running numbers, or one running XOR, can replace tracking every individual value.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write a correct hash set version; knowing both the sum formula and the overflow-safe XOR alternative is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: expected sum minus actual sum, or XOR every index and value together, either way present values cancel out.
